facts.quote: A market order is an order to buy or sell a stock at the best available price.  Generally, a market order will be executed immediately.
facts.claim: A market order buys or sells at the best price available and generally fills right away.

facts.quote: However, the price at which a market order will be executed is not guaranteed.
facts.claim: A market order's price is not guaranteed.

facts.quote: parts of a large market order may execute at different prices due to lack of liquidity at a price at the time of execution.
facts.claim: One large order can fill in parts, at several prices, when one price lacks enough shares.

facts.quote: A limit order is an order to buy or sell a stock at a specific price or better.
facts.claim: A limit order trades only at your price or better.

facts.quote: A buy limit order can only be executed at the limit price or lower, and a sell limit order can only be executed at the limit price or higher.
facts.claim: A buy limit fills at the limit or lower; a sell limit fills at the limit or higher.

facts.quote: A limit order is not guaranteed to execute.  A limit order can only be filled if the stock’s market price reaches the limit price.
facts.claim: A limit order may never fill.

facts.quote: A stop order, also referred to as a stop-loss order, is an order to buy or sell a stock once the price of the stock reaches a specified price, known as the stop price.
facts.claim: A stop order, also called a stop-loss order, acts once price reaches the stop price.

facts.quote: When the stop price is reached, a stop order becomes a market order.
facts.claim: At the stop price, a stop order turns into a market order.

facts.quote: buy stop order is entered at a stop price above the current market price. Investors generally use a buy stop order to limit a loss or to protect a profit on a stock that they have sold short.
facts.claim: A buy stop sits above the current price; investors generally use it to limit a loss or protect a profit on a short.

facts.quote: sell stop order is entered at a stop price below the current market price. Investors generally use a sell stop order to limit a loss or to protect a profit on a stock that they own.
facts.claim: A sell stop sits below the current price; it limits a loss or protects a profit on shares you own.

facts.quote: The stop price is not the guaranteed execution price for a stop order.  The stop price is a trigger that causes the stop order to become a market order.
facts.claim: The stop price is a trigger, not a promised fill price.

facts.quote: Investors should carefully select the stop price they use for a stop order since short-term market fluctuations in a stock’s price can activate a stop order.
facts.claim: Short-term swings can set off a stop, so choose the stop price with care.

facts.quote: Once the stop price is reached, a stop-limit order becomes a limit order that will be executed at a specified price (or better).
facts.claim: At the stop price, a stop-limit turns into a limit order.

facts.quote: As with all limit orders, a stop-limit order may not be executed if the stock’s price moves away from the specified limit price.
facts.claim: A stop-limit may not fill if price moves past its limit.

facts.quote: The stop price and the limit price for a stop-limit order do not have to be the same price.
facts.claim: A stop-limit's stop price and limit price can be different.

facts.quote: A trailing stop order is a stop or stop limit order in which the stop price is not a specific price.
facts.claim: A trailing stop's stop price is not a fixed number.

facts.quote: Instead, the stop price is either a defined percentage or dollar amount, above or below the current market price of the security
facts.claim: The trail is a set percent or dollar amount away from the market price.

facts.quote: As the price of the security moves in a favorable direction the trailing stop price adjusts or “trails” the market price of the security by the specified amount.
facts.claim: When price moves your way, the trailing stop follows it by the set amount.

facts.quote: However, if the security’s price moves in an unfavorable direction the trailing stop price remains fixed, and the order will be triggered if the security’s price reaches the trailing stop price.
facts.claim: When price moves against you, the trailing stop stays put and triggers if price reaches it.

facts.quote: The price of XYZ peaks at $24 then starts to drop (not in your favor).  Your trailing stop price will remain at $23.
facts.claim: In the SEC's example, a $1 trail under a $24 peak holds at $23 on the drop.

facts.quote: Investors should carefully select the trailing stop price they use for a trailing stop order since short-term market fluctuations in a stock’s price can activate a trailing stop order.
facts.claim: Short-term swings can set off a trailing stop.

facts.quote: Unless an investor specifies a time frame for the expiration of an order, orders to buy and sell a stock are “Day” orders, meaning they are good only during the trading day that the order is entered.
facts.claim: Unless you pick a time frame, an order is a Day order, good only for the day you enter it.

facts.quote: Day orders, if not executed, generally cancel at the end of regular trading hours of the trading day that they are entered and will not carry over to the extended hours session or the next trading day.
facts.claim: An unfilled Day order cancels at the close and does not carry into after-hours or the next day.

facts.quote: A GTC order is an order to buy or sell a stock that lasts until it is executed in full or it is canceled.
facts.claim: A GTC order lasts until it fills in full or is canceled.

facts.quote: the time limit that an investor can leave a GTC order open may vary based on the brokerage firm.
facts.claim: How long a GTC order can stay open varies by broker.

facts.quote: An IOC order is an order to buy or sell a stock that must be executed immediately.  Any portion of the order that cannot be filled immediately will be canceled.
facts.claim: IOC: fill what can fill right away and cancel the rest.

facts.quote: An FOK order is an order to buy or sell a stock that must be executed immediately in its entirety; otherwise, the entire order will be canceled
facts.claim: FOK: the whole order fills right away, or the whole order cancels.

facts.quote: (i.e., no partial execution of the order is allowed)
facts.claim: A fill-or-kill order never takes a partial fill.

facts.quote: An AON order is an order to buy or sell a stock that must be executed in its entirety, or not executed at all.
facts.claim: AON: the whole order or nothing.

facts.quote: However, unlike the FOK order, an AON order that is not executed immediately will remain active until it is executed or it is canceled.
facts.claim: Unlike FOK, an AON order that can't fill right away stays active.

facts.quote: A market or limit order that must be executed at the closing price. Any balance not executed as part of the closing trade is canceled.
facts.claim: An on-close order fills at the closing price; any part that misses the closing trade cancels.

facts.quote: A stop order may be triggered by a short-term, intraday price move that results in an execution price for the stop order that is substantially worse than the stock’s closing price for the day.
facts.claim: A quick intraday move can set off a stop and fill it far worse than the day's close.

facts.quote: The execution price an investor receives for this market order can deviate significantly from the stop price due to the prices of available liquidity when the market order executes.
facts.claim: A triggered stop can fill far from the stop price.

facts.quote: Unless you specify otherwise, your broker will enter your order as a market order.
facts.claim: If you don't say otherwise, your broker enters a market order.

facts.quote: “Price improvement” is the opportunity, but not the guarantee, for an order to be executed at a better price than the current quote.
facts.claim: A fill can come in better than the quote, but that is never promised.

facts.quote: A short sale is the sale of a stock that an investor does not own or a sale which is consummated by the delivery of a stock borrowed by, or for the account of, the investor.
facts.claim: A short sale sells stock you don't own, delivered with borrowed shares.

facts.quote: The investor later closes out the position by returning the borrowed security to the stock lender, typically by purchasing securities on the open market.
facts.claim: You close a short by buying the shares back and returning them to the lender.

facts.quote: Typically, when you sell short, your brokerage firm loans you the stock.
facts.claim: When you sell short, your broker usually lends you the shares.

facts.quote: your brokerage firm will charge you interest on the loan, and you are subject to the margin rules.
facts.claim: Borrowed shares cost interest, and the short is under the margin rules.

facts.quote: shorting a stock leaves an investor open to the possibility of unlimited losses, since a stock can theoretically keep rising indefinitely
facts.claim: A short's loss has no ceiling, because price can keep rising.

facts.quote: Regulation SHO requires a broker-dealer to have reasonable grounds to believe that the security can be borrowed so that it can be delivered on the date delivery is due before effecting a short sale order in any equity security.
facts.claim: Before a short sale, Regulation SHO requires reasonable grounds that the shares can be borrowed and delivered.

facts.quote: This “locate” must be made and documented prior to effecting the short sale.
facts.claim: The locate is made and documented before the short sale, not after.

facts.quote: The term “short squeeze” refers to the pressure on short sellers to cover their positions as a result of sharp price increases or difficulty in borrowing the security the sellers are short.
facts.claim: A short squeeze is pressure on shorts to cover, from a sharp rise or a hard borrow.

facts.quote: The rush by short sellers to cover produces additional upward pressure on the price of the stock, which then can cause an even greater squeeze.
facts.claim: Shorts rushing to cover push the price up more, which can squeeze harder.

facts.quote: Short interest is the aggregate number of open short sale positions.
facts.claim: Short interest is the total of open short positions.

facts.quote: claiming that there will be an imminent short squeeze, in which the alleged “naked” short sellers will be forced to cover open short positions at increasing prices. These claims in fact may be false.
facts.claim: Claims that a squeeze is about to happen may be false.

facts.quote: A market order generally will execute at or near the current bid (for a sell order) or ask (for a buy order) price.
facts.claim: A market buy generally fills at or near the ask; a market sell at or near the bid.

facts.quote: A broker or dealer may not accept a short sale order in an equity security from another person, or effect a short sale in an equity security for its own account, unless the broker or dealer has:
facts.claim: Under Rule 203, a broker may not take or make a short sale until a borrowing condition is met.

facts.quote: Reasonable grounds to believe that the security can be borrowed so that it can be delivered on the date delivery is due; and
facts.claim: One condition: reasonable grounds that the shares can be borrowed and delivered when delivery is due.

facts.quote: any buy order with a limit price equal to or greater than the national best offer at the time of order receipt, or any sell order with a limit price equal to or less than the national best bid
facts.claim: A marketable limit order is a buy limit at or above the best ask, or a sell limit at or below the best bid.

facts.quote: brokerage firms typically enter your order as a market order unless you specify otherwise.
facts.claim: Unless you say otherwise, brokers typically enter a market order.

facts.quote: This type of order provides the most certainty that your order will be executed because it's not tied to any restrictions.
facts.claim: A market order is the surest way to get a fill.

facts.quote: This is an order to buy or sell a security at or better than a specified price (a "limit price").
facts.claim: A limit order sets a limit price: that price or better.

facts.quote: This means you're guaranteed to get your limit price or a better price if your order is executed.
facts.claim: If a limit order fills, it fills at the limit price or better.

facts.quote: If you have a short position, you can generally use stop-buy orders to limit losses in the event the stock’s price increases.
facts.claim: On a short, a buy stop limits the loss if price rises.

facts.quote: With a buy stop order, you set a target price, and a market order to buy shares is automatically placed when the stock price hits your threshold.
facts.claim: A buy stop places a market buy when price rises to your level.

facts.quote: good ‘til canceled orders, which remain in effect until they’re executed by the brokerage firm or canceled by the customer
facts.claim: A GTC order stays in effect until it is executed or you cancel it.

facts.quote: market-on-open and market-on-close orders, which are executed as close as possible to the beginning or end of regular trading hours or canceled.
facts.claim: Market-on-close orders trade as close as possible to the end of regular hours, or cancel.

facts.quote: Market, limit and stop orders can include time mandates and other conditions.
facts.claim: Orders can carry time limits and other conditions.

facts.quote: the “stop price,” also known as a “trigger” price.
facts.claim: FINRA calls the stop price the trigger price.

facts.quote: if markets are volatile and stock prices are changing rapidly, your stop order may be executed at a price that’s significantly different from your stop price.
facts.claim: In a fast market a stop can fill far from the stop price.

facts.quote: Rapid price movement during a short period of time could trigger a stop order.
facts.claim: A brief, sharp move can set off a stop.

facts.quote: With this type of order, your shares will only be bought or sold once the stop price is reached if your brokerage firm can obtain the specified limit price or better.
facts.claim: A stop-limit trades only if the limit price or better is available after the stop is hit.

facts.quote: Consider using a stop limit order, rather than a stop order, if your primary goal is achieving a desired target price rather than getting an immediate execution irrespective of the price.
facts.claim: A stop-limit suits a price goal; a plain stop suits getting out whatever the price.

facts.quote: Because the investor does not own the shares, the brokerage firm will look to “locate” shares prior to executing the short sale.
facts.claim: The broker locates shares before it executes a short sale.

facts.quote: “Short interest” is a snapshot of the total open short positions existing on the books and records of brokerage firms for all equity securities on a given settlement date.
facts.claim: Short interest is a snapshot of open short positions on a set date.

facts.quote: short sale volume data is not the equivalent of short interest position data.
facts.claim: Short sale volume is not the same thing as short interest.

facts.quote: An executed order. Also, the price at which an order is executed.
facts.claim: A fill is an executed order, or the price it executed at.

facts.quote: The difference between estimated transactions costs and actual transactions costs. The difference usually represents revisions to price difference or spread and commission costs.
facts.claim: Slippage is the gap between the cost you expected and the cost you got, usually from changes in price, spread or commission.

facts.quote: Actual purchase of securities by a short seller to replace those borrowed at the time of a short sale.
facts.claim: Short covering is a short seller buying shares to replace the borrowed ones.

facts.quote: (OCO) order is a conditional order in which two orders are placed and one order is canceled if the other order is filled.
facts.claim: An OCO is two orders where one filling cancels the other.

facts.quote: bracket order immediately places an OCO "take profit" and a stop order after a position is opened.
facts.claim: A bracket places a linked take-profit and stop as soon as the position opens.

facts.quote: If a trader enters a long position, a bracket order immediately places an OCO sell limit (take profit) and sell stop.
facts.claim: On a long, a bracket's exits are a sell limit above and a sell stop below, linked as an OCO.

facts.quote: Durational means an order must take place within a specific time frame, or "time in force."
facts.claim: Time in force is the time frame an order must happen within.

facts.quote: A day order is canceled at the end of the day, while a GTC order remains active beyond the end of a trading day.
facts.claim: A day order cancels at the close; a GTC order stays active past it.

facts.quote: however long the broker will allow it to remain active (typically no more than 90 days) with a GTC order.
facts.claim: Schwab says brokers typically allow a GTC order no more than 90 days.

facts.quote: With a stop-limit order, a trader risks missing the market altogether.
facts.claim: A stop-limit can miss the market entirely.

facts.quote: Note that the trailing stop price for long positions doesn't adjust lower if the stock price drops.
facts.claim: On a long, a trailing stop never moves down.

facts.quote: the sell stop will immediately be canceled, removing the risk of inadvertently opening a short position should the stock decline to $36 or below.
facts.claim: Linking the exits as an OCO cancels the stop once the target fills, so it can't open a short by accident.

facts.quote: Two orders are placed simultaneously; if one order is executed, the other is canceled.
facts.claim: OCO: two orders live at once; one fills, the other cancels.

facts.quote: Once the stop (activation) price is reached, the trailing order becomes a market order, or the trailing stop limit order becomes a limit order.
facts.claim: A triggered trailing stop becomes a market order; a trailing stop-limit becomes a limit order.

facts.quote: Short selling involves borrowing a security whose price you think is going to fall and then selling it on the open market.
facts.claim: Short selling means borrowing shares and selling them, betting the price falls.

facts.quote: You may be able to short the most liquid shares for nothing, while the least liquid shares could come with an annualized interest rate of more than 100% of the value of your position.
facts.claim: Borrow costs run from nothing on liquid shares to very high yearly rates on scarce ones.

facts.quote: the cost to borrow a stock can change frequently in response to supply and demand conditions.
facts.claim: The cost to borrow can change often with supply and demand.

facts.quote: trigger a market order to buy back the shares at the next available price if the stock price rises to or above the stop price.
facts.claim: On a short, a buy stop sends a market buy if price rises to the stop.

facts.quote: specify a stop price that follows, or "trails," the lowest price of a stock by a percentage or dollar amount that you set.
facts.claim: A trailing buy stop follows the stock's lowest price by your set amount.

facts.quote: If the stock rises above its lowest price by the trail or more, it triggers a buy market order. If the price drops, the stop resets at a lower price.
facts.claim: A trailing buy stop triggers when price rises the trail amount off its low, and resets lower as price falls.

facts.quote: the stop order could lock in significant losses if the price gaps up.
facts.claim: A gap can carry a stop's fill far past the stop price.

facts.quote: Losses for short-sellers can be particularly heavy during a short-squeeze, which is when a heavily shorted stock unexpectedly rises in value, triggering a cascade of further price increases
facts.claim: Short losses can be heavy in a squeeze, when a heavily shorted stock jumps and keeps rising.

facts.quote: your broker may require you to deposit more cash or securities to cover the shortfall immediately.
facts.claim: A margin call asks you to deposit more cash or securities right away.

facts.quote: As the shorts scramble to buy back and cover their losses, upward momentum can build on itself, causing the stock to move sharply higher.
facts.claim: Shorts buying back to cover can drive the stock sharply higher.

facts.quote: Locating the shares can sometimes be difficult for your clearing firm because of high demand or a small number of outstanding shares.
facts.claim: Shares to borrow can be hard to find when demand is high or few shares exist.

facts.quote: The higher that percentage, the greater the bearish sentiment may be around that stock.
facts.claim: The higher short interest runs as a share of the float, the more bearish the crowd may be on the stock.

facts.quote: Decide how much money you would be comfortable losing in any trade ahead of time.
facts.claim: Decide your maximum loss before the trade.

facts.quote: marketable limit order is an order to buy (or sell) in which the limit price is at or above (or below) the current market.
facts.claim: A marketable limit is priced at or through the current market.

facts.quote: With a one-cancels-the-other order (OCO), 2 orders are live so that if either executes, the other is automatically triggered to cancel.
facts.claim: OCO: two live orders; when either executes, the other cancels.

facts.quote: They give you the ability to place both a protective stop loss order to minimize your losses and a limit order to maximize your gains.
facts.claim: An OCO lets a protective stop and a profit-taking limit sit on the same shares.

facts.quote: A one-triggers-the-other order actually creates both a primary and a secondary order. If the primary order executes, the secondary order automatically triggers.
facts.claim: OTO: when the first order executes, it triggers the second.

facts.quote: In a one-triggers-a-one-cancels-the-other order, you place a primary order which, if executed, triggers 2 secondary orders. If either of these secondary orders executes, the other is automatically canceled.
facts.claim: Fidelity's name for a bracket: the entry triggers two exits, and one filling cancels the other.

facts.quote: Limit orders for more than 100 shares or for multiple round lots (200, 300, 400, etc.) may be filled completely or in part until completed.
facts.claim: A limit order can fill in parts until it is complete.

facts.quote: Like any limit order, a stop limit order may be filled in whole, in part, or not at all, depending on the number of shares available for sale or purchase at the time.
facts.claim: A stop-limit can fill in whole, in part, or not at all.

facts.quote: Fidelity customers with a margin agreement in place may enter short sale and buy-to-cover orders for any U.S. stock using our online trading platform.
facts.claim: Short sale and buy to cover are the order actions that open and close a short.

facts.quote: Seller enters a buy to cover order at price B. If the price is above the price at which it was originally sold short (B1), the short seller generally realizes a loss.
facts.claim: Covering above the price you shorted at is a loss.

facts.quote: All short sale orders are subject to the availability of the stock being sold, which must be confirmed by our stock loan department prior to the order being entered.
facts.claim: A short needs available shares, confirmed before the order goes in.

facts.quote: you may be charged a short interest fee on the securities that you have borrowed to sell short and those fees may change, sometimes significantly without warning.
facts.claim: The fee on borrowed shares can change, sometimes a lot and without warning.

facts.quote: All open GTC orders will expire 180 calendar days after they are placed.
facts.claim: At Fidelity, open GTC orders expire after 180 calendar days.

facts.quote: Immediate or cancel (fill the whole order or any part immediately, and cancel any unfilled balance).
facts.claim: IOC fills all or any part at once and cancels the rest.

facts.quote: This limitation requires that the order is immediately completed in its entirety or canceled.
facts.claim: FOK: completed in full right away, or canceled.

facts.quote: You place a time limitation on a stock trade order by selecting one of the following time-in-force types
facts.claim: The time-in-force choice sets an order's time limit.

facts.quote: They can also be used to establish a position in a security if it reaches a certain price threshold or to close a short position.
facts.claim: Stop orders can open a position when price reaches a level, or close a short.

facts.quote: Buy stop loss and buy stop limit orders must be entered at a price which is above the current market price.
facts.claim: Buy stops must be entered above the current price.

facts.quote: Bracket orders are designed to help limit your loss and lock in a profit by "bracketing" an order with two opposite-side orders.
facts.claim: A bracket wraps an order with two opposite-side exits, one for loss and one for profit.

facts.quote: A BUY order is bracketed by a high-side sell limit order and a low-side sell stop order.
facts.claim: A buy's bracket is a sell limit above and a sell stop below.

facts.quote: In order to prevent a partial fill, the client uses an All-or-None order type, which can also be used for stock orders.
facts.claim: All-or-none is used to avoid a partial fill.

facts.quote: An order that uses the Good-Til-Canceled (GTC) time in force will continue to work until the order fills or is canceled
facts.claim: A GTC order keeps working until it fills or is canceled.

facts.quote: select a desirable time-in-force from the TIF dropdown menu.
facts.claim: Time in force (TIF) is a setting you pick on the ticket.

facts.quote: Slippage refers to the difference between the expected price of a trade and the price at which the trade is executed.
facts.claim: Slippage is the gap between the price you expected and the price you got.

facts.quote: Slippage can be positive, negative, or neutral, depending on the execution price.
facts.claim: Slippage can go for you, against you, or be zero.

facts.quote: It is most common in volatile or low-liquidity markets where prices can change rapidly.
facts.claim: Slippage is most common in fast or thin markets.

facts.quote: Investors can reduce the risk of negative slippage by using limit orders and avoiding highly volatile trading periods.
facts.claim: Limit orders and calmer periods reduce bad slippage.

facts.quote: Positive slippage means the investor gets a better price than expected, while negative slippage means the opposite.
facts.claim: Positive slippage is a better price than expected.

facts.quote: A one-cancels-the-other (OCO) order is a pair of conditional orders stipulating that if one order executes, then the other order is automatically canceled.
facts.claim: An OCO pairs two orders so one executing cancels the other.

facts.quote: OCO orders are commonly used in retracement- and breakout-based trading strategies, which let traders prepare for different market moves.
facts.claim: OCO orders are common in pullback and breakout trading, to be ready for either move.

facts.quote: A hard-to-borrow list identifies stocks that are hard to obtain for short sales.
facts.claim: Hard-to-borrow stocks are hard to get for short sales.

facts.quote: Stocks on this list might have higher loan fees due to limited availability.
facts.claim: Hard-to-borrow stocks can carry higher loan fees.

facts.quote: This alerts account holders that if they attempt to sell that security short, their trade order may be refused.
facts.claim: A short order in a hard-to-borrow stock may be refused.

facts.quote: Brokerage firms update their hard-to-borrow lists daily.
facts.claim: Brokers update their hard-to-borrow lists every day.

facts.quote: A heavy short interest does not mean that the price will rise. It means that many people believe it will fall.
facts.claim: Heavy short interest means many expect a fall; it does not mean a rise.

facts.quote: Anyone who buys in hopes of a short squeeze should have other (and better) reasons to think that the price of the stock will go higher.
facts.claim: Buying for a hoped-for squeeze needs a better reason than the squeeze.

facts.quote: Because short sellers exit their positions with buy orders, the coincidental exit of these short sellers pushes prices higher.
facts.claim: Shorts exit by buying, so many exiting at once pushes price up.

facts.quote: Most brokers set GTC orders to expire 30 to 90 days after investors place them to avoid a long-forgotten order suddenly being filled.
facts.claim: Investopedia says most brokers expire GTC orders after 30 to 90 days.

facts.quote: D48. Skip a short when the stock is hard to borrow or the borrow fee is high. ("48, yes.")
facts.claim: Our rule D48: we skip a short when the stock is hard to borrow or the borrow fee is high.

facts.quote: E57. Entries are market orders. ("57, No i market order everything.") The stop still sits with the broker (D41).
facts.claim: Our rule E57: we enter with market orders, and the stop still sits with the broker.

facts.quote: B23. Trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. ("23, yes.")
facts.claim: Our rule B23: we trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.

facts.quote: Default trail: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones; sell what is left on a close below it.
facts.claim: Our default trail: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones; a close below it sells what is left.

facts.quote: 9 and 20 EMA everywhere, with the 50 and 200 SMA.
facts.claim: D-021: the course uses the 9 and 20 EMA everywhere, with the 50 and 200 SMA.

facts.quote: Shorting is recommended only for traders who have already made $1 million trading.
facts.claim: We only recommend shorting to traders who have already made $1 million trading.

facts.quote: Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head.
facts.claim: Every position we hold has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in our head.
