facts.claim: The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider.

facts.quote: A stop cannot catch an overnight gap: a tight stop never licenses a monster position.
facts.claim: A stop can't catch an overnight gap, so a tight stop never justifies a monster position.

facts.quote: Every setup, long or short, enters as price trades through its trigger during the day, never at the close.
facts.claim: We enter every setup as price trades through its trigger during the day, never at the close.

facts.quote: No short-interest rule.
facts.claim: We have no short-interest rule.

walkthroughs.title: Market, limit, stop
steps: A market order says fill me now. You'll almost surely get filled. The price isn't promised. I market order my entries.
A limit order says my price or better. You control the price, but it might never fill.
A stop order sits and waits. When price hits the stop, it turns into a market order.
A stop-limit turns into a limit order instead. Your price is protected. Your fill isn't.

walkthroughs.title: How long it lives, how much fills
steps: Every order has a time in force. Don't pick one and it's a day order.
A day order that doesn't fill dies at the close. It won't carry into after-hours or tomorrow.
Good 'til canceled stays live until it fills or you cancel it. Your broker sets how long that can run.
IOC fills what it can right now and cancels the rest. FOK is all of it now, or nothing.

walkthroughs.title: Short words
steps: Shorting sells shares you don't own. Your broker lends them to you, and that loan can cost you.
Before you short, the broker needs a locate: good reason to believe the shares can be borrowed.
Close it by buying the shares back, a buy to cover. A crowd covering at once shoves price up: a short squeeze.
We only recommend shorting to traders who've already made $1 million trading.

questions.q: Your stock is trading through the level you marked last night. You hit buy at market. What did you just tell your broker?
choices: Trade now at the best price available
Trade only at my limit price or better
Trade once price hits my stop price
Trade at the day's closing price
questions.answer: Trade now at the best price available
questions.why: Fill me now, at the best price out there. That's all a market order says. You get the fill right away, but the price isn't promised. On a breakout that's the trade I want. I market order my entries, because missing the move costs more than a few cents. Where it bites is a fast or thin stock, where the fill can land above the price you saw.
questions.lesson_line: A market order buys you the fill, not the price.

wrong.Trade only at my limit price or better: That's a limit order. It protects your price, and on a breakout it can leave you watching the stock run.
wrong.Trade at the day's closing price: That's an on-close order, a separate instruction you'd have to pick.
wrong.Trade once price hits my stop price: That's a stop order. It waits for the stop price, then goes to market.

questions.simple: A market order says fill me now at the best price, so you get in fast but not at a set price.

reasons: fixed before (2026-11-10 variety rewrite)

deeper.example: The SEC says a market order generally executes right away, at a price that isn't guaranteed. FINRA calls it the surest way to get a fill.

questions.q: You type a share count into a new order ticket and never pick an order type. Most brokers will send that as a market order.
questions.why: True. Leave the type blank and most brokers send it at market. That's fine when you meant it. It's a problem when you thought you'd set a limit and the stock is moving fast. Then you pay whatever the market asks. Platforms differ, so look at what your own ticket defaults to. I read the order type and the time in force on every order before I send it.
questions.lesson_line: Read the order type before you send. Leave it blank and you likely get the market.
questions.simple: True. Pick no type and most brokers send a market order, so check your ticket before you hit send.

reasons: a broker convention ('typically'), not a rule; individual platform presets were not surveyed

deeper.example: FINRA and the SEC's glossary both say brokers typically enter a market order unless you specify otherwise. 'Typically' matters here: a platform can preset something else, which is why you check yours.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A buyer will pay $25.40 and not a cent more, so they use a ___ order.
questions.why: Limit. A limit order trades only at your price or better. For a buy, that means the limit price or lower, so $25.40 is the most the buyer pays. The trade-off: a limit order is not guaranteed to fill at all.
questions.lesson_line: A limit order names your price. The trade-off is that it may never fill.
questions.simple: Limit, because a buy limit can only fill at its price or lower, so the buyer never pays more than $25.40.

questions.q: Your sell limit sits at $30.00, above the market. The stock tops out at $29.90 and turns. Your order can fill at $29.90.
questions.why: False. A sell limit at $30.00 means $30.00 or better, and for a seller better is higher. $29.90 is a dime short, so nothing happens. You still own every share. That's the deal with a limit. You control the price, and you give up the sure fill. If getting out matters more than a dime, that's a market order's job.
questions.lesson_line: Buy limit: your price or lower. Sell limit: your price or higher.
questions.simple: False. A sell limit at $30.00 only sells at $30.00 or higher, and the stock never got past $29.90.

questions.q: You want a stock, but you won't pay over $52.00 for it. You put in a buy limit at $52.00. What is that $52.00?
choices: The most you'll pay per share
The price that triggers the order
The price you're sure to get
The last trade before you sent it
questions.answer: The most you'll pay per share
questions.why: It's the most you'll pay. A buy limit at $52.00 fills at $52.00 or lower, never higher. If a seller shows up under it, you get the better price. What it doesn't do is promise a fill. If the stock lifts off without trading at $52.00, you get nothing. For a sell it flips, and the limit is the least you'll take.
questions.lesson_line: The limit is your line in the sand. Better can happen. Worse can't.

wrong.The price that triggers the order: That's a stop price. A limit order is live the moment you send it.
wrong.The price you're sure to get: Nothing's sure. It can fill lower, or not fill at all.
wrong.The last trade before you sent it: That's the last sale. Your limit is a number you pick, not one the market hands you.

questions.simple: It's the most you'll pay. A buy limit fills at $52.00 or lower, but it may not fill at all.

questions.q: What kind of limit order did you just send?
questions.story: The quote reads $10.00 bid, $10.05 ask. You want in now, but you won't pay up much. You send a buy limit at $10.10.
choices: Marketable: it can fill right away
Non-marketable: it waits for a seller
A stop-limit waiting on a trigger
Non-marketable: it fills only at $10.10
questions.answer: Marketable: it can fill right away
questions.why: Marketable. Your $10.10 limit is above the $10.05 ask, so it reaches the sellers sitting there and can fill right away. It still caps you. A buy limit fills at the limit or lower, so the worst you pay is $10.10, a nickel over the ask. That's the point of it. You get most of the speed of a market order, with a ceiling on the price.
questions.lesson_line: A buy limit at or above the ask is marketable. It acts fast and still caps your price.

wrong.Non-marketable: it waits for a seller: That's a buy limit under the ask, at the bid for example. Yours already reaches the sellers.
wrong.A stop-limit waiting on a trigger: There's no stop price here. It's a plain limit, live the second you send it.
wrong.Non-marketable: it fills only at $10.10: A buy limit fills at the limit or lower, not only at it. Above the $10.05 ask, it can trade at once.

questions.simple: Marketable. A buy limit above the ask can fill right away, and you still never pay more than $10.10.

deeper.example: The SEC's rule text defines a marketable limit order as a buy limit priced at or above the best offer. Marketable is judged when the order arrives, against the best offer then.

questions.q: You bought a stock at $50 and park a sell stop at $48 with your broker. What does that order actually do?
choices: Becomes a market order at a trigger
Fills only at your price or better
Cancels unless it is filled right away
Sells at exactly the stop price shown
questions.answer: Becomes a market order at a trigger
questions.why: It waits, then goes to market. Nothing happens while the stock trades over $48. The moment it trades at $48, the stop turns into a market order and sells. You get whatever the market pays right then, so the fill can come in under $48. That's still the order I want sitting there. Every position we hold has a real stop with the broker, not one in our head. A stop in your head gets talked out of.
questions.lesson_line: A stop is a trigger. Once it fires, you get the market.

wrong.Fills only at your price or better: That's a limit order. A stop has no price floor once it fires.
wrong.Sells at exactly the stop price shown: $48 is the trigger, not a promise. A fast drop fills you lower.

questions.simple: A stop waits for its price, then turns into a market order, so the fill can come in under $48.

reasons: choices rewritten in the 2026-11-10 variety pass

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Another name for a stop order is a ___ order.
questions.why: Stop-loss. The SEC says a stop order is 'also referred to as a stop-loss order'. Same order, two names. A stop-limit is a different order: at the stop price it becomes a limit order, not a market order.
questions.lesson_line: Stop and stop-loss name the same order.
questions.simple: Stop-loss, because the SEC says a stop order is also called a stop-loss order.

reasons: the key rests on one cited fact (SEC f7, Tier 1)

questions.q: Your stop sits at $63.40, a few cents under the low of the day. What is that $63.40?
choices: The price that sets the order off
The price your shares will sell at
The worst price you'll accept
Your average cost on the trade
questions.answer: The price that sets the order off
questions.why: It's the trigger. $63.40 is the price that sets the order off, nothing more. Once the stock trades there, your stop becomes a market order and sells at whatever's bid. On a calm day that's close. On a fast flush it can be a lot lower. We put it a few cents under the low of the day because that's where the chart says we're wrong. The number tells the broker when, not what you'll get.
questions.lesson_line: Stop price means trigger. It's not the price you get.

wrong.The price your shares will sell at: Not promised. The stop turns into a market order, and the fill can be worse.
wrong.The worst price you'll accept: That's a limit price. A plain stop has no limit.
wrong.Your average cost on the trade: That's your cost. The stop goes where the chart says you're wrong.

questions.simple: It's the trigger. When the stock trades at $63.40 the stop goes to market, and the fill can be lower.

deeper.example: FINRA calls the stop price the 'trigger' price. The SEC says it's not the guaranteed execution price.

questions.q: You bought a stock at $40 and your stop sits at $38.80. That caps your loss at $1.20 a share.
questions.why: False. $40 minus $38.80 is the $1.20 you planned to risk. It's not a cap. A stop decides when you get out, not the price. Bad news overnight, and the stock can open well under $38.80. Your stop fires at the open and sells there. A stop can't catch an overnight gap. That's why a tight stop never justifies a monster position. Size it so a gap stings but doesn't wreck the account.
questions.lesson_line: The name sounds like a promise. It's a trigger, and gaps and fast markets go right through it.
questions.simple: False. The stop sets when you sell, not the price, so a gap or a fast drop can fill you well under $38.80.

deeper.trap: The name 'stop-loss' sounds like a cap on the loss. It is not. FINRA warns that in volatile markets a stop may be executed at a price significantly different from the stop price. Schwab notes a short's stop could lock in significant losses if the price gaps up. The stop decides when you get out, not the price you get.

reasons: fixed before (why sentence split)

questions.q: A stock trades at $74. You want an order that sits up at $76 and buys only if price rises to it. Which order is that?
choices: Buy stop
Buy limit
Sell stop
Sell limit
questions.why: A buy stop. It sits at $76, above where the stock trades, and does nothing until price climbs there. Then it goes to market and buys. That's how you get long only if the stock proves itself through a level. It's also the stop on a short. Don't grab a buy limit for this. A buy limit at $76 with the stock at $74 fills right away, because $74 is already under your limit.
questions.lesson_line: A buy stop waits above the price. A rise to it fires a market buy.

wrong.Buy limit: A buy limit at $76 fills at $76 or lower. With the stock at $74, it buys right now.
wrong.Sell stop: A sell stop sits below the price and sells. Wrong side, wrong direction.
wrong.Sell limit: A sell limit sells at your price or higher. It never turns into a buy.

questions.simple: A buy stop. It waits above the price and buys at market only if the stock rises to $76.

questions.q: Which order do you put in?
questions.story: You're short a stock at $30. If it rips up to $31, you want out automatically, with no watching the screen.
choices: Buy stop at $31
Sell stop at $31
Buy limit at $31
Sell limit at $31
questions.why: Buy stop at $31. You're short, so getting out means buying the shares back. A buy stop sits above the price and fires as a market buy if the stock rises to $31. Put it in the moment you're short. A stock can keep going up, so a short's loss has no ceiling. That makes the stop the most important order on the trade. In a fast squeeze the fill can still come in over $31.
questions.lesson_line: Short a stock and your stop is a buy stop above. Set it when you enter.

wrong.Sell stop at $31: A sell stop sells and sits below the price. You're short, so out means buying.
wrong.Buy limit at $31: With the stock under $31, a buy limit at $31 buys right away. You'd cover now, not on a rise.
wrong.Sell limit at $31: You own no shares. Selling at $31 shorts more instead of getting you out.

questions.simple: A buy stop at $31. You close a short by buying, and a buy stop fires only on a rise.

questions.q: Do you still own the shares?
questions.story: Your sell stop sits at $45. At 10 a.m. the stock dips to $44.80 for a few minutes, then rallies hard. It closes at $47.
choices: No, the stop sold on the dip
Yes, stops wait for the close
No, they sold at the $47 close
Yes, the dip was too quick
questions.answer: No, the stop sold on the dip
questions.why: No. The stop sold you on the dip. A stop doesn't wait for the close. The moment the stock traded at $45, your order went to market and sold, somewhere between $45 and $44.80. The rally to $47 happens without you. That stings, but that's the stop doing its job. You control where it goes. Put it where the chart says you're wrong, not where a normal wiggle tags it.
questions.lesson_line: A stop doesn't wait for the close. A brief dip through it is enough to set it off.

wrong.Yes, stops wait for the close: A stop fires when price trades there during the day. It doesn't wait for the close.
wrong.No, they sold at the $47 close: The dip set it off at $45, and it sold right then. The close came hours later.
wrong.Yes, the dip was too quick: A few minutes at $44.80 is plenty to set it off. The close came too late to matter.

questions.simple: No. A stop fires as soon as price trades there, so a few minutes at $44.80 sold you out.

deeper.trap: A $47 close makes the $45 stop look safe. It was not. The SEC warns a short-term, intraday move can trigger a stop. The fill can be substantially worse than the day's close. So choose the stop price with care.

questions.q: Your broker's ticket offers Stop and Stop Limit. You pick Stop Limit on a stock you own. What does it do?
choices: Turns into a limit at the stop
Stays live until you cancel it
Follows the price up as it rises
Fills all of it or none of it
questions.answer: Turns into a limit at the stop
questions.why: It turns into a limit order. The stop price says when, the limit price says how bad a fill you'll take. Once the stock trades at your stop, a limit order goes in and sells only at your limit or better. That protects your price. The catch is the fill. If the stock drops straight through your limit, nothing sells and you're still holding it. When the job is getting out of a loser, the sure exit matters more than the price.
questions.lesson_line: Stop-limit: the stop says when, the limit says how bad a price you'll take.

wrong.Stays live until you cancel it: That's good 'til canceled, a time setting, not an order type.

questions.simple: It turns into a limit order at the stop, so it guards your price but may not sell in a fast drop.

reasons: choices rewritten in the 2026-11-10 variety pass

questions.q: How do you set up the exit?
questions.story: You own 300 shares trading at $42. You want out if it drops to $40. But you won't sell under $39.50, even if that means no sale.
choices: Sell stop-limit: stop $40, limit $39.50
Sell a plain stop order at $40, no limit
Sell limit at $39.50, as a day order
Sell trailing stop with a $0.50 trail
questions.why: Sell stop-limit, stop $40, limit $39.50. The $40 sets it off. Then a limit order goes in that sells only at $39.50 or better. That's exactly what you asked for. Just know the cost. If the stock gaps or flushes through $39.50, nothing sells and you're holding it lower. You traded the sure exit for a floor on price.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-limit has two prices: the stop sets it off, and the limit guards the price.

wrong.Sell limit at $39.50, as a day order: With the stock at $42, that limit is already beaten. It sells right now, not at $40.
wrong.Sell trailing stop with a $0.50 trail: That rides $0.50 under the price and moves up. It's not the $40 trigger you asked for.
wrong.Sell a plain stop order at $40, no limit: That goes to market at $40. In a fast drop it can sell under $39.50, which you said you won't take.

questions.simple: A stop-limit. At $40 it becomes a limit order that won't sell under $39.50, even if that means no sale.

deeper.trap: A stop-limit can leave you holding a falling stock. FINRA says it trades only if the limit price or better can be had after the stop is hit. Schwab warns that with a stop-limit a trader risks missing the market altogether. If the stock drops through $39.50 fast, this order sits unfilled while the loss grows.

reasons: fixed before (Sell prefix restored on the key)

questions.q: Your protective order is a sell stop-limit. The stock gaps down through both prices at the open. You can still be holding it.
questions.why: True. Once the stop price trades, a stop-limit becomes a limit order. If the stock opens under your limit, that order just sits there unfilled. You still own it, and it's falling. That's the trade-off. A stop-limit protects your price. A plain stop gets you out at whatever the market pays. For us the stop is the exit, so know which one you've got in before the drop comes.
questions.lesson_line: If getting out matters most, a stop-limit can fail you. Know which one you've got in.
questions.simple: True. Once triggered it's a limit order, and if price opens below your limit it never fills.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking a stop-limit is a safer stop. It protects the price, not the exit. In a fast drop or a gap through both prices, the limit is left behind. You can still hold the stock after it falls. Schwab warns that with a stop-limit a trader risks missing the market altogether. FINRA says to choose a stop-limit when the price matters more than getting out.

questions.q: You're up nicely on a trade and your broker offers a 'trailing stop'. What does that order do?
choices: A stop that follows price by a gap
A stop parked at your entry price
A stop that only counts at the close
A stop that turns into a limit order
questions.answer: A stop that follows price by a gap
questions.why: It follows price by a set gap. You pick a dollar amount or a percent. As the stock rises, the stop rises with it and keeps that distance. When the stock dips, the stop stays put, and it fires if price falls back to it. That locks in part of a gain without you touching anything. Our own trail is different. We trail under the 9 or 20 EMA and sell on a close below it.
questions.lesson_line: A trailing stop moves one way only: in your favor.

wrong.A stop parked at your entry price: A stop at your entry is a fixed level. A trailing stop follows price only when it moves your way.
wrong.A stop that only counts at the close: Stops trigger when price reaches them during the day.
wrong.A stop that turns into a limit order: That's a stop-limit. A plain trailing stop becomes a market order. What makes it trailing is that its stop price follows the market.

questions.simple: It follows the price up by a set gap and holds still on dips, so it locks in part of a gain.

reasons: fixed before (stop-limit note reworded)

questions.q: You buy at $40 with a sell trailing stop $2 under the price. It runs to $47.40, then dips to $46. Where's your stop now?
questions.why: $45.40. A trailing stop hangs off the high, not your entry. $47.40 minus the $2 trail is $45.40. When the stock dips to $46, the stop doesn't follow it down. It holds at $45.40, and $46 is still above it, so nothing fires. Your stop now sits well over your $40 entry. Short of a gap, this one can't turn into a loser. That's the broker's version. Our own trail is the 9 or 20 EMA, on a close.
questions.lesson_line: A trailing stop tracks the high, not your entry.
questions.simple: $45.40. It trails the $47.40 high by $2 and doesn't drop on the dip to $46.

reasons: computed key (calc)

wrong.$38.00: That's $2 under your $40 entry. The trail follows the high, not where you bought.
wrong.$47.40: That's the high itself. You forgot to take off the $2.
wrong.$44.00: That trails the $46 dip. The stop never moves down on a dip.

questions.q: You own a stock with a sell trailing stop under it. It has a rough red day and drops. Your trailing stop moves down with it.
questions.why: False. A sell trailing stop only moves one way, and that's up. On a red day it stays exactly where it was. If the stock falls far enough to reach it, it fires. That's the whole point of it. It never gives back ground it already took. If it slid down with the stock, it wouldn't be protecting anything.
questions.lesson_line: Up, it follows. Down, it waits for you at the line.
questions.simple: False. A sell trailing stop only moves up with the stock, and it stays put when the stock falls.

questions.q: What's wrong with this setup?
questions.story: You put a sell trailing stop $0.25 under the price. The stock swings about $2 on a normal day. You plan to hold it for weeks.
choices: Small dips will trigger it
It waits for the day's close
It turns into a limit order
It moves down on red days
questions.why: Small dips will trigger it. A $0.25 trail on a stock that swings about $2 a day sits deep inside its normal range. Any wiggle after a new high takes you out. That's a weeks-long plan killed by ordinary noise. A swing trade needs a stop the normal daily range can't reach. That's why we trail under the 9 or 20 EMA and sell on a close below it, not on a tick.
questions.lesson_line: A trail tighter than the stock's normal swing gets hit by ordinary noise.

wrong.It turns into a limit order: A plain trailing stop becomes a market order when it fires.
wrong.It moves down on red days: It never moves down. On a drop it holds still.
wrong.It waits for the day's close: It fires when price reaches it during the day. With a trail that tight, almost any dip does that.

questions.simple: Small dips will trigger it. A $0.25 trail is far tighter than the stock's normal $2 daily swing.

deeper.trap: A tight trail feels safer because it gives back less. But the SEC says short-term fluctuations can activate a trailing stop. If the stock swings about $2 a day, a $0.25 trail gets hit by ordinary noise. Once triggered, a plain trailing stop becomes a market order. The SEC's advice is to select the trailing stop price carefully.

questions.q: Where does your buy stop trigger?
questions.story: You're short at $40 with a $2 trailing buy stop. The stock falls to a low of $31, then bounces.
choices: At $33
At $42
At $38
At $31
questions.why: At $33. On a short the trail hangs off the low. $31 plus the $2 trail is $33. As the stock fell from $40, the stop came down with it, from $42 to $33. It doesn't climb back up on the bounce. So a pop to $33 covers you, and you keep most of the drop. Everything on a short is flipped. A long's trail rides under the highs, a short's rides over the lows.
questions.lesson_line: On a short the trail follows the lows. Every new low pulls your stop down.

wrong.At $31: That's the low itself. The stop sits the $2 trail above it.
wrong.At $42: That's $2 over your $40 entry, where it started. It came down as the stock fell.
wrong.At $38: That's your entry minus the trail. On a short the stop sits above the price, and it trails the low.

questions.simple: At $33. On a short the trail sits $2 above the lowest price, and the low was $31.

deeper.trap: On a short, everything flips. A long's trailing stop rides under the highs. A short's trailing buy stop rides above the lows. As the stock falls from $40 to $31, the stop falls with it, from $42 to $33. It never climbs back on the bounce, so a bounce of $2 or more off the low triggers it.

reasons: computed key (calc)
trailing buy stop mechanics come from one Tier 2 publisher (Schwab f86, f87); the SEC f17 covers the general trail

questions.q: Your broker offers a 'bracket order' on the ticket. What does a bracket put in for you?
choices: An entry with linked stop and target
Two orders where one cancels the other
A stop that follows the price up
An order to buy within a price range
questions.answer: An entry with linked stop and target
questions.why: An entry with a stop and a target attached. You send one ticket. When the entry fills, a sell stop goes in below and a sell limit above, and they're linked. If one fills, the other cancels. The big win is your stop is in the second you're filled. There's no window where you hold a position with no protection.
questions.lesson_line: A bracket puts the whole plan on the ticket: entry, stop, target.

wrong.Two orders where one cancels the other: That's an OCO. A bracket uses one for its exits, but it starts with the entry.
wrong.An order to buy within a price range: The name sounds like a range, but it isn't one. It's one entry with a linked stop and target.

questions.simple: An entry with a stop and a profit target attached, linked so when one exit fills the other cancels.

reasons: choices rewritten in the 2026-11-10 variety pass

deeper.example: Schwab and Interactive Brokers call it a bracket. Fidelity calls the same thing one-triggers-a-one-cancels-the-other (OTOCO): the entry triggers two exits, and one filling cancels the other.

questions.q: What did you just send?
questions.story: A stock trades at $25.40. You send one ticket: buy 200 shares at market. When it fills, a sell limit at $28.00 and a sell stop at $24.20 go in, linked.
choices: Bracket order
Trailing stop
Stop-limit order
Fill-or-kill
questions.why: A bracket. One ticket, three orders. The market buy fills near $25.40. Then the $28.00 target and the $24.20 stop go in together, linked. Whichever fills first cancels the other. That link keeps you from selling the same shares twice and ending up short by accident. And your stop is live from the first second you own the stock.
questions.lesson_line: With a bracket, the stop is in the moment you're filled.

wrong.Trailing stop: A trailing stop is one exit that moves with price. This ticket has an entry and two fixed exits.
wrong.Stop-limit order: A stop-limit is one order with two prices. This is three linked orders.
wrong.Fill-or-kill: Fill-or-kill is a size and timing condition: all of it now, or cancel.

questions.simple: A bracket. One ticket buys, then puts in a linked profit target and a stop.

deeper.example: Fidelity calls the same structure one-triggers-a-one-cancels-the-other. Interactive Brokers describes a bracket as an order wrapped by two opposite-side orders, one for the loss and one for the profit.

questions.q: You own 300 shares with a sell stop below and a sell limit above. Your broker offers to link them as OCO. What does that do?
choices: Two orders: one fills, other cancels
One order: all of the shares or none
One order fills, then triggers a second
Cancels if not filled right away
questions.answer: Two orders: one fills, other cancels
questions.why: One fills, the other cancels. Here's why that matters. Say the stock runs to your sell limit and sells all 300. Without the link, your stop is still sitting there. If the stock later drops through it, the stop sells shares you don't own anymore. Now you're short by accident. OCO kills the stop the moment the target fills.
questions.lesson_line: OCO keeps your two exits from both firing.
questions.simple: It links your two exits, so when one fills the other cancels and you can't sell the same shares twice.

questions.q: Tap the order link that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: My target and my stop cover the same 300 shares, linked as an ___ so one fill kills the other.
questions.why: OCO, one-cancels-the-other. Your target and your stop both cover the same 300 shares. Linked as an OCO, the stop is canceled as soon as the target fills. Without the link, a stop left behind could later sell shares you no longer own and open a short by accident.
questions.lesson_line: Two exits on one position: link them as an OCO.
questions.simple: OCO is the link, because it cancels the stop once the target fills, so both exits never fire.

questions.q: How do you set up the two entries?
questions.story: A stock trades at $21. You'll buy a pullback to $20 or a breakout over $22.50, whichever comes first. You want one position, not two.
choices: OCO of buy limit $20, stop $22.50
Buy limit $20, buy stop $22.50
A bracket on the $20 buy limit
One stop-limit, $20 to $22.50
questions.why: An OCO, a buy limit at $20 and a buy stop at $22.50. Whichever fills first cancels the other. Without the link, a pop to $22.50 and a drop back to $20 fills both. Now you hold double your plan. For what it's worth, I don't park entries like this. We market order our entries as price trades through the trigger. But if you leave orders working while you're away, this keeps it to one position.
questions.lesson_line: An OCO links two orders so only one of them can fill.

wrong.Buy limit $20, buy stop $22.50: Separate orders can both fill. A pop to $22.50, then a drop to $20, doubles the position.
wrong.A bracket on the $20 buy limit: A bracket hangs exits on one entry. It doesn't cancel the breakout entry.
wrong.One stop-limit, $20 to $22.50: A buy stop sits above the price and $20 is below it. One order can't be both entries.

questions.simple: An OCO. It links both entries so when one fills the other cancels, and you end up with one position.

deeper.trap: Two separate entry orders aren't linked. If the stock pops to $22.50 and then drops back to $20, both fill and the position is twice the plan. An OCO pairs them, so one filling cancels the other.
deeper.example: Investopedia notes OCO orders are common in retracement and breakout trading, to be ready for either move.

reasons: fixed before (f123 claim)
teaches resting limit and stop entries beside the owner's rule E57 (entries are market orders): flagged

questions.q: Next to the price on every order ticket is a 'time in force' box, set to DAY on most of them. What does that box control?
choices: How long the order stays live
The price that triggers it
How many shares can fill
When the trade settles
questions.answer: How long the order stays live
questions.why: How long the order stays live. DAY means today only. If it hasn't filled by the close, it's gone. GTC means it stays working until it fills or you cancel it, within your broker's time limit. This matters most on stops. A stop you meant to keep for weeks, sent as a day order, is gone tomorrow. Then you're holding with no protection and don't know it.
questions.lesson_line: Every order has a clock. Check it before you send.

wrong.The price that triggers it: That's the stop price, its own field on a stop order. Time in force is about how long the order lives.
wrong.How many shares can fill: That's the quantity, plus size conditions like all-or-none.
wrong.When the trade settles: Time in force is the time frame the order itself must happen within. It sets nothing about settlement.

questions.simple: Time in force sets how long your order stays live, like today only or until you cancel it.

reasons: choices rewritten in the 2026-11-10 variety pass; rebalanced again here

questions.q: You send a limit order and leave time in force alone. If it doesn't fill, it's gone after today's close.
questions.why: True. Pick nothing and it's a day order, good only for the session you send it in. Unfilled at the close, it cancels. It doesn't carry into after-hours or tomorrow. If you still want the trade the next day, you send it again. That's also why your protective stop should be GTC. We keep a real stop with the broker on every position, and a day stop is gone overnight.
questions.lesson_line: No time limit chosen means today only.
questions.simple: True. With no time in force picked it's a day order, and it cancels at today's close if it hasn't filled.

questions.q: Did you get the shares?
questions.story: At 2 p.m. you place a day order to buy at a $30.00 limit. It doesn't fill by the close. After hours, the stock trades at $29.80.
choices: No, it expired at the close
Yes, it filled after hours at $29.80
No, it waits for tomorrow's open
Yes, it bought at market at the close
questions.answer: No, it expired at the close
questions.why: No. It died at the close. A day order is only good for the regular session you send it in. Unfilled by the bell, it cancels. It doesn't carry into after-hours or the next day. So the $29.80 print after the close can't touch it, even though it's under your $30.00 limit. If you still want the shares, send a new order. Check your open orders after the close so you know what's really working.
questions.lesson_line: A day order dies at the close. If you still want it, enter it again.

wrong.Yes, it filled after hours at $29.80: A day order doesn't carry into after-hours. It was gone at the close.
wrong.No, it waits for tomorrow's open: That's what a GTC order would do. A day order doesn't carry to the next day.
wrong.Yes, it bought at market at the close: A limit order never turns into a market order. Unfilled at the close, it cancels.

questions.simple: No. An unfilled day order cancels at the close, so the after-hours trade at $29.80 can't fill it.

deeper.trap: The trap is seeing a price below your $30.00 limit after hours and assuming you bought. The SEC says day orders that don't execute generally cancel at the end of regular trading hours. They don't carry over to the extended hours session. Check your open orders after the close. A day order that missed is gone, not waiting.

questions.q: You set a stop at $88 that you mean to keep for weeks, and you mark it GTC. What does GTC tell your broker?
choices: Live until filled or you cancel
Live only for today's session
Fill right away or cancel at once
Live for the rest of this week
questions.answer: Live until filled or you cancel
questions.why: Keep it live until it fills or I cancel it. That's good 'til canceled. Unlike a day order, it survives the close and is still there tomorrow. That's what you want on a protective stop. You set it once, and it guards the position every day you hold. Your broker does put a time limit on it, so know yours.
questions.lesson_line: GTC outlives the day. Keep track of what you've left working.

wrong.Live only for today's session: That's a day order. Your $88 stop would be gone tomorrow.
wrong.Live for the rest of this week: GTC isn't a set week. It runs until it fills or you cancel.

questions.simple: GTC keeps the order live past today, until it fills or you cancel it, so your stop stays in.

questions.q: You put in a GTC order months ago and never canceled it. It can still have expired on its own.
questions.why: True. Good 'til canceled isn't forever. Each broker sets its own limit. Fidelity cancels open GTC orders after 180 calendar days. Schwab puts the norm at no more than 90 days. So a stop you set long ago may be gone. Or an order you forgot about may still be live. Either one can hurt you, so look over your open orders every so often.
questions.lesson_line: Good 'til canceled isn't forever. Know your broker's limit.
questions.simple: True. Brokers put a time limit on GTC orders, and it varies, so an old order can expire.

deeper.trap: An order you set months ago may be gone, or may still be live. Fidelity cancels open GTC orders after 180 calendar days. Investopedia says most brokers expire them after 30 to 90 days, to avoid a long-forgotten order suddenly being filled. Review what you have working.

reasons: broker time limits (180 days, 90 days) can change; no number is keyed
re-asked as True in wave8 to drop the absolute-word tell

questions.q: Buying 800 shares, you send the order immediate-or-cancel (IOC). Only 300 can fill right away. How many get canceled?
questions.why: 500. IOC grabs what it can right now and cancels the rest. 800 minus the 300 that filled is 500 canceled, and you keep the 300. Fill-or-kill would have canceled all 800. So after an IOC, look at what you actually own. Your stop has to cover the 300 you hold, not the 800 you asked for.
questions.lesson_line: IOC takes what's there now and walks away from the rest.
questions.simple: 500. IOC keeps the 300 it can fill now and cancels the rest of the 800.

deeper.counter: A fill-or-kill order on the same ticket would cancel all 800 shares. The SEC says FOK allows no partial execution: the whole order fills at once or none of it does. IOC keeps the 300 it could get.

reasons: computed key (calc)

choices: 500 shares
800 shares
1,100 shares
300 shares

wrong.800 shares: That cancels the whole order. That's fill-or-kill, not IOC.
wrong.1,100 shares: You added the filled shares to the order instead of taking them off.
wrong.300 shares: That's what filled, and you keep those. The other 500 are what get canceled.

questions.q: What do you put on the ticket?
questions.story: You want 5,000 shares. You'll take them only if all 5,000 fill right now. Otherwise, forget it.
choices: Fill-or-kill (FOK)
Immediate-or-cancel (IOC)
All-or-none (AON)
Good 'til canceled (GTC)
questions.why: Fill-or-kill. All 5,000 right now, or the whole order cancels. No partial. IOC would keep whatever part filled. All-or-none also refuses a partial, but it sits and waits. You said now or never, and that's FOK. We market order our entries, so you won't need these often. Know them when you see them on the ticket.
questions.lesson_line: FOK: all of it, right now, or nothing.

wrong.Immediate-or-cancel (IOC): IOC keeps whatever part fills right away. You could end up with a partial.
wrong.All-or-none (AON): AON wants all of it too, but it can sit and wait. You said now or never.
wrong.Good 'til canceled (GTC): GTC is about how long the order lives. It says nothing about filling all at once.

questions.simple: Fill-or-kill. It buys all 5,000 shares right now or cancels the whole order.

questions.q: Where does each order stand a second later?
questions.story: You send two orders to buy 1,000 shares. Only 400 are offered at your price right now. Order A is fill-or-kill. Order B is all-or-none.
choices: A cancels, B waits for all 1,000
Both buy 400 and cancel the rest
A buys 400 now, B cancels at once
Both wait until all 1,000 can fill
questions.answer: A cancels, B waits for all 1,000
questions.why: A cancels, B waits. Only 400 of your 1,000 are on offer. Fill-or-kill needs all 1,000 right now, so it cancels on the spot. All-or-none needs all 1,000 too, but it's allowed to wait. It stays working until the full size shows up or you cancel it. Both refuse a partial. Only FOK refuses to wait.
questions.lesson_line: FOK and AON both refuse a partial. Only FOK refuses to wait.

wrong.Both buy 400 and cancel the rest: That's immediate-or-cancel. Neither of these takes a partial.
wrong.Both wait until all 1,000 can fill: Fill-or-kill can't wait. It cancels at once if it can't fill in full.
wrong.A buys 400 now, B cancels at once: Backwards. Fill-or-kill never takes a partial, and all-or-none is the one that can wait.

questions.simple: A cancels at once, because fill-or-kill can't wait. B waits, because all-or-none can stay open for all 1,000.

deeper.trap: Both orders refuse a partial fill, so it is easy to treat them as the same. The difference is time. The SEC says an FOK must execute immediately in its entirety. An AON that can't fill right away remains active until it is executed or canceled. All or nothing, but able to wait: AON. All or nothing, right now: FOK.

questions.q: Tap the order that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: I want my buy filled at the end of today's regular session, so I'll send a ___ order.
questions.why: Market-on-close. It is an order to be executed at the closing price. Any part not executed in the closing trade is canceled. Market-on-open is the same idea at the start of regular trading hours.
questions.lesson_line: On-close orders trade the closing price, or not at all.
questions.simple: Market-on-close is the order meant to fill at the day's closing price, and any unfilled part cancels.

questions.q: You sent a buy at market. Your order screen now reads FILLED, 200 at $41.06. What does 'filled' mean there?
choices: It traded, and that's your price
An order still waiting to trade
Shares left after a cancel
The total shares traded today
questions.answer: It traded, and that's your price
questions.why: Your order traded. A fill is a done trade, or the price it got done at. So you own 200 at $41.06. That's the number your risk runs from, not the price you saw before you hit buy. Your stop distance and your size come off the fill. Until it says filled, you don't own anything. It's just an order.
questions.lesson_line: A fill is a done trade. Until then, it's just an order.

wrong.Shares left after a cancel: Those didn't fill. A fill is what did trade.
wrong.The total shares traded today: That's the day's volume, for everyone. A fill is your own order.
wrong.An order still waiting to trade: That's a working order. Nothing has traded yet.

questions.simple: Your order traded. A fill is a done trade or its price, so you own 200 at $41.06.

reasons: the key rests on one cited fact (Nasdaq f68, Tier 1)
fixed before (circular wrong note reworded)

questions.q: You market buy 5,000 shares into a fast breakout. That one order can fill at several different prices.
questions.why: True. A big order eats through the offers. If the ask doesn't hold all 5,000, your order takes what's there and moves up to the next price, then the next. That's several fills on one order. What counts is your average fill. Run your stop distance and your size off that, not off the first print you saw.
questions.lesson_line: Big order, thin price: expect several fills and check the average.
questions.simple: True. When one price doesn't have all 5,000 shares, your order fills the rest at the next prices up.

questions.q: Your order status reads PARTIAL. What happened to your order?
choices: Only part of your order executed
Your order filled at a worse price
Your broker refused the order
Your order filled after the close
questions.answer: Only part of your order executed
questions.why: Only part of it traded. Some shares filled, and the rest didn't. What happens to the rest depends on the order. IOC cancels it at once. An unfilled day order cancels at the close. GTC keeps working it. Either way, check what you own before you set your stop. A stop sized for shares you never got can leave you short when it fires.
questions.lesson_line: Check the filled shares, not just the order. A partial can leave you half in.

wrong.Your order filled at a worse price: That's slippage. An order can fill in full and still fill worse.
wrong.Your broker refused the order: That's a rejected order. Nothing filled.
wrong.Your order filled after the close: That's an after-hours fill. It says nothing about how much filled.

questions.simple: Only part of your order traded, and the rest was canceled or is still waiting.

questions.q: What do you call what happened?
questions.story: A trader says after the open: "Only got 300 of my 1,000 before it ran from my limit." Nothing else filled.
choices: Partial fill
Slippage
Rejected order
Fill-or-kill
questions.why: A partial fill. 300 of the 1,000 traded at the limit or better, then the stock ran off. A limit never chases, so the rest just sat there. The price was fine. The size fell short. That's the cost of a limit on a runner. It's one reason we market order our entries. On a breakout I'd rather pay a few cents more than own a third of what I planned.
questions.lesson_line: A limit protects your price, so on a runner you may get only part.

wrong.Slippage: Slippage is a worse price than expected. Here the price was fine. The size fell short.
wrong.Rejected order: A rejected order fills nothing. This one got 300 shares.
wrong.Fill-or-kill: A fill-or-kill order would have canceled. It never takes part of an order.

questions.simple: A partial fill. Only 300 of the 1,000 shares traded before the price ran from the limit.

deeper.trap: Don't call this slippage. Slippage is about price, a fill better or worse than you expected. Here the price was fine and the size fell short. The cure differs too. Limit orders reduce bad slippage, while a partial fill is the price a limit order pays for its control. Then check whether the rest of the order is still working.

questions.q: Where do you stand now?
questions.story: Your GTC limit order to buy 2,000 shares has 600 filled. The stock then moved up and away from your limit.
choices: You own 600, 1,400 still working
Done, the other 1,400 canceled
You own 2,000 at an average price
Nothing counts until all 2,000 fill
questions.why: You own 600, and 1,400 are still working at your limit. A GTC order lasts until it fills in full or you cancel it. A plain limit can fill in parts, so the 600 are yours and the rest waits. Here's the catch. Weeks from now the stock can come back and fill the other 1,400, after your reason to buy is gone. So decide now. Leave it working on purpose, or cancel it.
questions.lesson_line: After a partial, decide: leave the rest working or cancel it. Don't forget it's there.

wrong.You own 2,000 at an average price: Only 600 traded. You don't own shares that never filled.
wrong.Nothing counts until all 2,000 fill: That's all-or-none. A plain limit order can fill in parts.
wrong.Done, the other 1,400 canceled: That's how a day order ends at the close, or an IOC right away. A GTC keeps working.

questions.simple: You own 600. The other 1,400 stay open at your limit, because a GTC order lasts until it fills or you cancel.

deeper.trap: The forgotten remainder. A GTC order keeps working after a partial. Weeks later the other 1,400 shares can fill when price comes back, maybe after your reason to buy is gone. The SEC notes that how long a GTC order can stay open varies by broker. After a partial, decide on purpose: keep the rest working or cancel it.

questions.q: You expected to buy at $35.10. Your fill came back at $35.18. What's the name for that difference?
choices: Slippage
The spread
The day's range
A gap
questions.why: Slippage. That's the gap between the price you expected and the price you got. Here you paid a few cents over the $35.10 you planned on. On a breakout bought at market, a little slippage is normal, and I accept it. What I watch is when it gets big. That tells you the stock is too thin or too fast for the size you're trading.
questions.lesson_line: Slippage measures your fill against the price you expected.

wrong.The spread: The spread is the gap between the bid and the ask. Slippage is your fill against what you expected.
wrong.The day's range: That's the day's high minus its low. It isn't about your order.
wrong.A gap: A gap is a jump on the chart between two days. It can cause slippage on a stop, but it isn't slippage.

questions.simple: Slippage. It's the gap between the price you expected and the fill you actually got.

reasons: fixed before (f69 claim)
two published definitions (conflicts note); the key uses the price sense both cover

deeper.example: Investopedia defines slippage as the difference between a trade's expected price and its executed price. Nasdaq frames it as the difference between expected and actual cost.

questions.q: You market buy 1,000 shares with the ask at $15.20. They fill at an average of $15.29. What did slippage cost you?
questions.why: $90. A market buy fills at or near the ask, so $15.20 was your expected price. You paid $15.29 on average. $15.29 minus $15.20 is $0.09 a share. Times 1,000 shares is $90. That's not a disaster, but it's real money, and it comes straight off your risk budget. Build your stop distance from the fill, not the quote.
questions.lesson_line: A big market order can fill at several prices. Check your average fill, not just the quote.
questions.simple: $90. You paid $15.29 a share instead of the $15.20 ask, on 1,000 shares.

reasons: computed key (calc)
fixed before (why reworded for an average fill)

wrong.$0.09: That's the slippage per share. You skipped the 1,000 shares.
wrong.$15,290: That's the total you paid, not the extra cost.

questions.q: You send a market buy with the ask at $22.40 and get filled at $22.37. That's slippage too, just in your favor.
questions.why: True. Slippage is any gap between the price you expected and the one you got. It cuts both ways. $22.37 is three cents better than the $22.40 ask, so this time it paid you. Enjoy it, but never plan on it. I plan risk on the worse fill and treat a better one as a bonus.
questions.lesson_line: Hope for better fills. Plan for worse ones.
questions.simple: True. Slippage is any gap from the price you expected, and this time the fill came in better.

deeper.counter: Positive slippage is real, but you can't plan on it. Investopedia notes slippage is most common in volatile or thin markets. The SEC calls a fill better than the quote price improvement, an opportunity but not a guarantee.

questions.q: Which stop is most likely to fill well past its price?
questions.story: You hold four stocks, the same size in each. Each has a sell stop the same distance under its price.
choices: A thinly traded stock on big news
A heavily traded stock on big news
A thinly traded stock on a quiet day
A heavily traded stock on a quiet day
questions.answer: A thinly traded stock on big news
questions.why: The thin stock on big news. A stop is just a trigger for a market order, and that order takes whatever bids are there. Fast price and few bids is the worst mix. The stock blows through your stop, and the next real bid can be way under it. That's one reason we only trade stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. Liquid names fill you close to your stop when it counts.
questions.lesson_line: Slippage is most common when price moves fast and few orders are there.

wrong.A heavily traded stock on big news: Fast, but deep. Speed is there, but there are plenty of bids to catch it.
wrong.A thinly traded stock on a quiet day: Thin, but calm. Few bids, but nothing is rushing through them.
wrong.A heavily traded stock on a quiet day: Deep and calm. Neither cause of slippage is there.

questions.simple: The thin stock on big news. Slippage is worst when price moves fast and few orders are there.

deeper.trap: The same stop distance doesn't mean the same risk. FINRA warns a stop in a fast market may fill significantly different from its stop price. In a thin stock on big news, the fill can land well past the stop.
deeper.example: Investopedia says slippage is most common in volatile or low-liquidity markets. The SEC says a triggered stop fills at the prices of available liquidity.

reasons: judgment key: no source ranks speed against thinness, so the key is the only choice with both (conflicts note)

questions.q: A stock you hate is breaking down, and a friend says to short it. What would you actually be doing?
choices: Selling borrowed shares, rebuy later
Selling shares on the day you buy them
Selling at a loss to cut risk
Selling part of a winning position
questions.why: Selling shares you borrowed, to buy them back later. Your broker lends you the shares and you sell them. If the price drops, you buy them back cheaper, return them, and keep the difference. If it rises, you lose, and there's no ceiling on how far it can rise. The borrowed shares cost you a fee too. One thing before you ever try it. We only recommend shorting to traders who have already made $1 million trading.
questions.lesson_line: Short means you sold first. You still owe the shares back.

wrong.Selling shares on the day you buy them: That's a day trade. You owned those shares first.
wrong.Selling at a loss to cut risk: That's taking a loss on shares you own.
wrong.Selling part of a winning position: That's selling partials, trimming shares you own.

questions.simple: You sell borrowed shares now and buy them back later, hoping the price falls.

reasons: fixed before (f103 added)

questions.q: Before your short sale can go through, your broker has to confirm the shares can be borrowed. What's that check called?
choices: Locate
Margin call
Short interest
Buy to cover
questions.why: A locate. Before your broker lets you sell shares you don't own, it needs good reason to believe it can borrow them and deliver them on time. That's the SEC's Regulation SHO. It happens before the short, not after. You only notice it when there's nothing to locate and your short order gets refused.
questions.lesson_line: No shares to borrow, no short.

wrong.Margin call: A margin call asks you to add cash or securities when your account falls short.
wrong.Short interest: Short interest is the total of open short positions in a stock.
wrong.Buy to cover: That's the order that closes a short.

questions.simple: A locate. The broker checks the shares can be borrowed before your short goes through.

reasons: a regulation that can change (Rule 203 of Regulation SHO; current eCFR text cited)

questions.q: Your broker can line up the locate after your short sale fills, as long as it's done the same day.
questions.why: False. Locate first, short second. Under the SEC's Regulation SHO the broker needs good reason to believe it can borrow the shares before it takes your short. Lining them up later that day doesn't fix it. So if your broker can't find shares, you don't get the short. That's the law, not your broker being difficult.
questions.lesson_line: The locate comes first. Then the short.
questions.simple: False. The broker has to be confident the shares can be borrowed before your short goes through.

reasons: a regulatory rule (Regulation SHO Rule 203) that can change; current eCFR text cited

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A short seller sells shares they don't own, so they first ___ them, usually from their broker.
questions.why: Borrow. A short sale is delivered with borrowed shares, and your broker usually lends them to you. The loan can carry a fee. Schwab says the most liquid shares may cost nothing and the least liquid more than 100% a year.
questions.lesson_line: A short starts with a loan of shares. Check what the borrow costs.
questions.simple: Borrow, because you sell shares you do not own, so you borrow them first, usually from your broker.

questions.q: You pull up a stock to short, and your platform flags it 'hard to borrow'. What's that telling you?
choices: Few shares free to lend for shorts
Shorting it is banned by law
It can't trade until the open
It's too costly to buy outright
questions.answer: Few shares free to lend for shorts
questions.why: Few shares are free to lend. Either a lot of shorts already borrowed them, or there just aren't many shares around. So the fee to borrow can be high, and your short order may be refused. The list changes every day. For us it's simple. Hard to borrow, or a high borrow fee, and we skip the short. A crowded short can squeeze hard, and you'd be paying up to sit in it.
questions.lesson_line: Hard to borrow can mean a higher fee to short, or a short order refused.

wrong.Shorting it is banned by law: It's about the broker's supply of shares to lend, not a law. A short may still go through, at a higher fee.
wrong.It can't trade until the open: The borrow has nothing to do with trading hours.
wrong.It's too costly to buy outright: Buying doesn't need a borrow. The flag is only about shorting.

questions.simple: Few shares are free to lend for shorts, so the fee can be high or your short refused.

reasons: fixed before ('can be high' restored)

questions.q: What most likely changed overnight?
questions.story: You try to short a heavily shorted stock. Your broker rejects the order. Yesterday the same order went through.
choices: Hard to borrow
Partial fill
Negative slippage
Time in force
questions.why: It went hard to borrow. In a heavily shorted stock, the shares to lend can run out. Brokers update that list every day, so yesterday's short can be today's rejection. Read the rejection message to be sure, since a broker can refuse a short for other reasons too. And if it's the borrow, we pass. We skip a short when the stock is hard to borrow.
questions.lesson_line: On a crowded short, the borrow can vanish from one day to the next. Check it before you plan the trade.

wrong.Partial fill: Nothing filled. The order was refused.
wrong.Negative slippage: Slippage needs a fill. Yours never traded.
wrong.Time in force: Time in force sets how long an order lives. It doesn't get a short refused.

questions.simple: Hard to borrow. When shares to lend run out, the broker can refuse a short, and that can change overnight.

deeper.trap: A stock you shorted easily last week can be closed to new shorts today. Brokers update hard-to-borrow lists daily. Schwab notes shares can be hard to locate when demand is high or few shares exist. A broker can also refuse a short for other reasons, such as no margin agreement. Read the rejection message.

reasons: hard-to-borrow status changes daily; hedged 'most likely' key because other refusal causes exist (conflicts note)

questions.q: You short a stock with a 2% yearly borrow fee. That fee is locked in until you cover.
questions.why: False. Borrow fees move with supply and demand, and they can change often. Fidelity warns they can jump a lot, with no warning. So the 2% you saw on day one can climb while you sit in the trade. Check the rate while you hold the short, not just when you put it on. A high borrow fee is a reason we skip a short in the first place.
questions.lesson_line: Check the borrow rate while you hold a short, not just when you enter.
questions.simple: False. The fee to borrow can change while you're short, sometimes a lot and with no warning.

questions.q: You're short 200 shares and you're done with the trade. Which order action gets you out?
choices: Buy to cover
Sell to close
Sell short
Buy to open
questions.why: Buy to cover. You sold first, so you get out by buying the 200 shares back and returning them. On the ticket, sell short opens it and buy to cover closes it. Pick the wrong one and you make it worse. Sell short again and you've doubled the short. Get the action right before you hit send.
questions.lesson_line: Sell short to open. Buy to cover to close.

wrong.Sell short: That sells more borrowed shares and makes the short bigger.
wrong.Sell to close: You own no shares to sell. You owe 200, and you close that by buying them back.
wrong.Buy to open: You're closing a short, not opening anything. Buy to cover is the action that closes it.

questions.simple: Buy to cover. You close a short by buying the 200 shares back.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: It ran against my short, so I bought the shares back to ___ at a loss.
questions.why: Cover. Buying shares back to close a short is short covering. You bought back above the price you shorted at, so covering locked in a loss.
questions.lesson_line: Covering is the buy that ends a short.
questions.simple: Cover is the word, because buying shares back to close a short is called covering.

questions.q: You short 200 shares at $18.00. A squeeze hits and you buy to cover at $27.40. How much did you lose, before costs?
questions.why: $1,880. On a short you lose what the price rises. $27.40 minus $18.00 is $9.40 a share. Times 200 shares is $1,880, before borrow costs. And $27.40 wasn't a ceiling. A short's loss has none, which is why the buy stop goes in the second you're short. With a stop a few percent over $18.00, this is a small loss instead.
questions.lesson_line: A short loses as price rises, and price can keep rising. Have your buy stop in.
questions.simple: $1,880. The price rose from $18.00 to $27.40, which is $9.40 a share on 200 shares.

reasons: computed key (calc)

wrong.$9.40: That's the loss per share. You skipped the 200 shares.

questions.q: A heavily shorted stock pops on news and keeps ripping all day. Someone calls it a short squeeze. What's happening?
choices: Short covering lifts the price fast
Shorts piling in sink the price
A stock stuck in a tight range
A broker forcing longs to sell
questions.answer: Short covering lifts the price fast
questions.why: Shorts are buying back, and their buying lifts it faster. Every short has to buy to get out. When the price jumps, a lot of them want out at once. Their buy orders push it higher, which squeezes the next group of shorts. It feeds on itself. That's why you never want to be the short who's late to the door.
questions.lesson_line: In a squeeze, the shorts become the buyers.

wrong.A stock stuck in a tight range: That's a tight range. Nobody is being forced to buy.
wrong.A broker forcing longs to sell: That's forced selling by owners. A squeeze is pressure on short sellers to buy back.
wrong.Shorts piling in sink the price: That's the reverse. In a squeeze the shorts are buying back, and that lifts the price.

questions.simple: Shorts rush to buy back, and their buying pushes the price up even faster.

reasons: choices rewritten in the 2026-11-10 variety pass

deeper.example: The SEC defines a short squeeze as pressure on short sellers to cover, from a sharp price rise or a hard borrow. Their rush to cover can cause an even greater squeeze.

questions.q: A stock you're watching has heavy short interest. That means a short squeeze is coming.
questions.why: False. Heavy short interest means a lot of people think it's going down. That's it. A squeeze needs something to force them out, like a sharp move up or the borrow drying up. Plenty of heavily shorted stocks just keep falling. Squeeze stories sell, and the SEC warns those claims can be false. I want a real reason to own a stock, like the chart and its relative strength. A crowd of shorts isn't one.
questions.lesson_line: Short interest is a crowd, not a catalyst. I'd want a real reason to own it.
questions.simple: False. Heavy short interest only shows many people expect a fall, and nothing forces them to buy.

deeper.trap: Squeeze stories sell. The SEC warns of claims that an imminent short squeeze will force shorts to cover. It says these claims in fact may be false. Investopedia adds that anyone buying for a squeeze should have other, better reasons to think the price will rise. A crowded short is a crowd's opinion, not a catalyst.

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: You're short a heavily shorted stock. It gaps up on news and keeps climbing as shorts buy back. It's just under your buy stop now.
choices: Let the stop take you out
Cancel the stop and wait it out
Raise the stop a bit to give it room
Wait for the close to decide
questions.answer: Let the stop take you out
questions.why: Let the stop take you out. This is exactly what it's there for. Shorts buying back push the price higher, and that can squeeze even harder. A short's loss has no ceiling. Canceling or raising the stop piles on risk right when it's growing. A stop never gets wider. In a move this fast the fill may come in over your stop. Take it anyway. Being stubborn in a squeeze is how accounts get hurt.
questions.lesson_line: On a short, honor the buy stop. A squeeze can keep running, and the loss has no ceiling.

wrong.Cancel the stop and wait it out: That removes your only exit while the loss has no limit.
wrong.Wait for the close to decide: A stop doesn't wait for the close, and neither does a squeeze.
wrong.Raise the stop a bit to give it room: That widens the loss you set before the trade. A stop never gets wider.

questions.simple: Let the stop close it. A squeeze can keep pushing price up, and a short's loss has no limit.

deeper.trap: The urge in a squeeze is to hold for a pullback, or to short more at a better price. Both raise risk while shorts are being forced to buy. The SEC notes their rush to cover can cause an even greater squeeze. Schwab's advice is to decide how much you'd be comfortable losing before the trade, then let the order you placed do its job.

reasons: judgment key that agrees with the owner's rulebook A4 and D41 (the stop is the exit, a real stop order with the broker)

questions.q: You look up a stock and see short interest of 40 million shares. What's that number counting?
choices: Total open short positions in a stock
Shares sold short in a single day
The yearly fee to borrow a stock
Shares the company bought back
questions.answer: Total open short positions in a stock
questions.why: Every short position still open in that stock. That's 40 million shares sold short and not yet bought back, as of one settlement date. It's a snapshot, not a live number. Don't mix it up with daily short volume. That's how many shares were sold short in a single day, a different number. For us it's background. We don't have a short-interest rule.
questions.lesson_line: Short interest counts positions still open. Daily short volume is a different number.

wrong.Shares sold short in a single day: That's short sale volume. It isn't the same as short interest.
wrong.The yearly fee to borrow a stock: That's the borrow fee, the interest on the stock loan.
wrong.Shares the company bought back: That's a buyback. It has nothing to do with shorts.

questions.simple: It counts the short positions still open in the stock, as of one date.

reasons: fixed before ('per day' fee note corrected)

deeper.example: The SEC calls short interest the aggregate number of open short positions. FINRA says it's a snapshot on a given settlement date, and that short sale volume is a different thing.

questions.q: Next week the stock trades down to $47.50. What happens?
questions.story: Your order screen shows: Sell 200 shares, type Stop, stop price $47.50, time in force GTC. The stock closes today at $49.
choices: It turns into a market sell order
Nothing, it expired at today's close
It sells exactly at $47.50 a share
It becomes a limit order at $47.50
questions.answer: It turns into a market sell order
questions.why: It turns into a market sell. Read both fields. GTC means the stop lives past today until it fills or you cancel, so it's still there next week. Stop means that at $47.50 it goes to market and sells. The fill can come in under $47.50, and on a gap down it can be well under. This is what you want on every position. A real stop with the broker that doesn't vanish at the close.
questions.lesson_line: Read the order type and the time in force together. They decide what happens, and when.

wrong.Nothing, it expired at today's close: That's what a day order would do. This one is GTC.
wrong.It sells exactly at $47.50 a share: The stop price is a trigger, not a promised price.
wrong.It becomes a limit order at $47.50: That's a stop-limit. The type here is a plain stop.

questions.simple: It becomes a market sell. GTC keeps the stop alive past today, and the stop fires at $47.50.

deeper.trap: Two fields decide this order: the type and the time in force. Read only the type and you might think it died at today's close. Read only the price and you might expect exactly $47.50. If the stock gaps below $47.50, the fill can land well under the stop.

reasons: choices rewritten in the 2026-11-10 variety pass

questions.q: What's this order doing?
questions.story: Your order screen shows: Buy to cover 100 shares, type Stop, stop price $31.00. The stock trades at $28.50.
choices: Protecting a short from a rise
Buying a fresh breakout above $31
Covering the short right now
Shorting more if it hits $31
questions.answer: Protecting a short from a rise
questions.why: It protects a short from a rise. Buy to cover only closes a short, so you're short 100 shares. The stop sits above the price and buys only if the stock climbs there. At $28.50 nothing happens. If it rises to $31.00, it goes to market, buys back the 100 and closes the short. That's a short's protective stop. 'Buy' on the screen doesn't always mean a new long.
questions.lesson_line: Buy to cover with a stop above the price: that's a short's protective stop.

wrong.Covering the short right now: It's a stop. It waits, and only buys if the stock rises to $31.
wrong.Buying a fresh breakout above $31: A breakout entry would be a plain buy. Buy to cover only closes a short.
wrong.Shorting more if it hits $31: Adding to a short takes a sell short order. Buy to cover only closes one.

questions.simple: It guards a short. A buy to cover stop above the price buys back only if the stock climbs to $31.00.

deeper.trap: 'Buy' on the screen doesn't always mean a new long. Buy to cover only closes shares you're short. Read the action and the type together: buy to cover plus stop, above the price, is a short's protective stop. FINRA says buy stop orders on a short limit losses if the price rises.

reasons: fixed before (rekeyed from 'Capping the loss')

questions.story: You plan to short a stock on a breakdown. Your broker flags it as hard to borrow.
questions.q: Do you still take the short?
choices: No, skip it on this stock
Yes, and count the fee in
Yes, once the locate clears
No, skip every short in its group
questions.answer: No, skip it on this stock
questions.why: No, skip it. Hard to borrow, or a high borrow fee, and we pass on the short. The broker can refuse the order, and the fee can jump while you hold. A stock few people can borrow is also a stock that can squeeze. There are other names showing the same weakness without that baggage. And remember, we only recommend shorting to traders who have already made $1 million trading.
questions.lesson_line: Hard to borrow or a high borrow fee: we skip the short.
questions.simple: No. We skip a short when the stock is hard to borrow, because of the fee and the squeeze risk.

wrong.Yes, and count the fee in: We don't price the fee in. A high borrow fee is a reason we skip the short.
wrong.Yes, once the locate clears: A locate only says shares can be found. We still skip a hard-to-borrow short.
wrong.No, skip every short in its group: It's about this stock's borrow. Other names in the group can still be fine.

reasons: house rule D48 (owner, 2026-11-09)
new in wave8

questions.q: You've sold some of a big winner and you're trailing the rest. What gets you out of what's left?
choices: A close below the 9 or 20 EMA
Its first touch of the 9 EMA
A trailing stop a set percent under it
A stop moved up under each day's low
questions.answer: A close below the 9 or 20 EMA
questions.why: A close below the 9 or 20 EMA. A fast mover we trail under the 9. A steadier one gets the 20. We sell what's left on a close below it, not on an intraday touch. Touches happen all the time in a healthy trend, and selling them shakes you out of the big leg. Waiting for the close makes the stock prove it's really breaking. A broker's trailing stop order fires on a touch, so it's not how we trail.
questions.lesson_line: We trail with the 9 or 20 EMA and sell on a close below it.

wrong.A trailing stop a set percent under it: That's the broker's trailing stop order. Our trail is the 9 or 20 EMA, on a close.
wrong.A stop moved up under each day's low: That trails way too tight for a winner. We use the 9 or 20 EMA and sell on a close below.
wrong.Its first touch of the 9 EMA: Touches happen all the time in a healthy trend. We wait for a close below.

questions.simple: A close below the 9 or 20 EMA. We sell on a close under it, not on a touch.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E52)

conflicts: GTC time limits differ by broker and by source: the SEC bulletin says the limit 'may vary based on the brokerage firm'; Fidelity's FAQ says open GTC orders expire after 180 calendar days; Schwab says brokers typically allow no more than 90 days; Investopedia says most brokers use 30 to 90 days. No question keys a number. q30's why and w2 say 'within your broker's time limit', and q31 keys only that the limit varies.

Default order type: FINRA's Order Types page and the SEC's Market Order glossary both say brokers typically enter a market order unless you specify otherwise. Individual platforms' ticket presets were not surveyed, so q02 is keyed on the official wording ('typically') and its why tells the member to check their own ticket.

Slippage has two published definitions. Nasdaq's glossary (Tier 1): the difference between estimated and actual transaction costs, 'usually' from price difference or spread and commission revisions. Investopedia (Tier 2): expected price vs executed price. Every slippage key uses the price sense, which Nasdaq's 'price difference' covers; the commission is never offered as a wrong answer for what slippage is, so neither definition is contradicted.

Bracket naming: Schwab and Interactive Brokers call entry-plus-linked-exits a 'bracket'; Fidelity calls the same structure one-triggers-a-one-cancels-the-other (OTOCO). Questions use 'bracket' and cite Fidelity's OTOCO text as the same structure (q23).

Trailing stop wording: the SEC bulletin defines a trailing stop as 'a stop or stop limit order'; Schwab's advanced-orders article says trailing stops 'are not orders per se' but a way to move stops. The file follows the SEC definition; q17's distractor 'A stop that turns into a limit order' is explained as the stop-limit definition, since what makes a stop trailing is the moving price (a trailing stop-limit exists, per the SEC and thinkorswim pages).

Outdated lines seen and NOT used: Fidelity's FAQ short-sale example says 'Three trading days later, on settlement date' and Nasdaq's 'Execution' glossary says stocks settle in three days (US settlement has been T+1 since May 2024); the SEC Key Points page says the locate is 'usually done two days before settlement' (written for T+2); Investopedia's squeeze page speaks of short positions' 'expiration date' (a stock short has none). No fact or question relies on them.

Stop triggers: the SEC says some firms trigger stops on last-sale prices and others on quotes. q13's story has the stock trade at $44.80 for a few minutes, through a $45 sell stop, so the key holds under either standard; no question asks which standard a broker uses.

Locate sources: the SEC's 'Key Points About Regulation SHO' page (last modified 2022) explains the locate in plain words; the current rule text (eCFR, 17 CFR 242.203(b)(1)) is cited beside it so the rule is checked as it stands today. Both say the same thing: the borrow condition comes before the short sale.

Rejected short (q50): a broker can also refuse a short order for reasons the unit does not teach (for example the Rule 201 short-sale price test, or an account without margin). None of those is a choice, and among the four words offered only hard to borrow can block a short, so the question asks which word 'most likely' explains it.

Slippage judgment (q44): the sources name two drivers, fast markets (FINRA, SEC, Investopedia) and thin liquidity (Investopedia, SEC 'prices of available liquidity'). No source ranks them, so the key is the only choice with both; each wrong choice carries one driver or neither, and its note says which.
